claim: Understanding the activity of the mammalian brain requires an integrative knowledge of circuits at distinct scales, ranging from ion channel gating to circuit connectomics.
source: Understanding the activity of the mammalian brain requires an integrative knowledge of circuits at distinct scales, ranging from ion channel gating to circuit connectomics.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for understanding brain activity, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Computational models are regularly employed to understand how multiple parameters contribute synergistically to circuit behavior.
source: Computational models are regularly employed to understand how multiple parameters contribute synergistically to circuit behavior.
evidence: This statement reflects established practice in neuroscience research.

claim: Traditional models of anatomically and biophysically realistic neurons are computationally demanding, especially when scaled to model local circuits.
source: However, traditional models of anatomically and biophysically realistic neurons are computationally demanding, especially when scaled to model local circuits.
evidence: This is a well-known limitation in computational neuroscience.

claim: The authors trained several artificial neural network (ANN) architectures to model the activity of realistic multicompartmental cortical neurons.
source: To overcome this limitation, we trained several artificial neural network (ANN) architectures to model the activity of realistic multicompartmental cortical neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: An ANN architecture was identified that accurately predicted subthreshold activity and action potential firing.
source: We identified an ANN architecture that accurately predicted subthreshold activity and action potential firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental results.

claim: The ANN could correctly generalize to previously unobserved synaptic input, including in models containing nonlinear dendritic properties.
source: The ANN could correctly generalize to previously unobserved synaptic input, including in models containing nonlinear dendritic properties.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated through testing on novel input conditions.

claim: When scaled, processing times were orders of magnitude faster compared with traditional approaches.
source: When scaled, processing times were orders of magnitude faster compared with traditional approaches, allowing for rapid parameter-space mapping in a circuit model of Rett syndrome.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from runtime comparisons.

claim: The ANN approach allows for rapid parameter-space mapping in a circuit model of Rett syndrome.
source: When scaled, processing times were orders of magnitude faster compared with traditional approaches, allowing for rapid parameter-space mapping in a circuit model of Rett syndrome.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the application to Rett syndrome modeling.

claim: Computational modeling has become a cornerstone technique for deriving and testing new hypotheses about brain organization and function.
source: Computational modeling has become a cornerstone technique for deriving and testing new hypotheses about brain organization and function (Sejnowski et al., 1988; Wolpert and Ghahramani, 2000; Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Our mechanistic understanding of neural function has evolved from describing action potential-related ion channel gating to constructing models that can simulate the activity of whole-brain regions in little more than 60 years.
source: In little more than 60 years, our mechanistic understanding of neural function has evolved from describing action potential (AP)-related ion channel gating (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952) to constructing models that can simulate the activity of whole-brain regions (Traub et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2013; Neymotin et al., 2016b; Chavlis et al., 2017; Turi et al., 2019).
evidence: This historical progression is supported by citations spanning from 1952 to 2019.

claim: The lack of available or affordable hardware for neural simulations currently represents a significant barrier to entry for most neuroscientists.
source: Although tremendous advancements have been made in the development of computational resources, the lack of available or affordable hardware for neural simulations currently represents a significant barrier to entry for most neuroscientists and renders many questions intractable.
evidence: This is presented as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Detailed single-cell models have been a regular occurrence in publications since the 1990s.
source: In contrast to detailed single-cell models, which have been a regular occurrence in publications since the 1990s (De Schutter and Bower, 1994; Mainen et al., 1995; Migliore et al., 1995; Mainen and Sejnowski, 1996; Destexhe et al., 1998; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Aradi and Holmes, 1999; Migliore et al., 1999), parallel simulation of thousands, or even hundreds of thousands of detailed neurons have only become a possibility with the advent of supercomputers (Markram et al., 2015; Bezaire et al., 2016; Arkhipov et al., 2018; Joglekar et al., 2018; Schmidt et al., 2018; Antolík et al., 2019; Schwalger and Chizhov, 2019; Billeh et al., 2020).
evidence: This historical observation is supported by multiple citations from the 1990s.

claim: Parallel simulation of thousands or hundreds of thousands of detailed neurons have only become a possibility with the advent of supercomputers.
source: In contrast to detailed single-cell models, which have been a regular occurrence in publications since the 1990s (De Schutter and Bower, 1994; Mainen et al., 1995; Migliore et al., 1995; Mainen and Sejnowski, 1996; Destexhe et al., 1998; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Aradi and Holmes, 1999; Migliore et al., 1999), parallel simulation of thousands, or even hundreds of thousands of detailed neurons have only become a possibility with the advent of supercomputers (Markram et al., 2015; Bezaire et al., 2016; Arkhipov et al., 2018; Joglekar et al., 2018; Schmidt et al., 2018; Antolík et al., 2019; Schwalger and Chizhov, 2019; Billeh et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent large-scale simulation studies.

claim: Several attempts have been made to mitigate the immense computational load of large-scale neural simulations by judicious simplification.
source: As these resources are still not widely accessible, several attempts have been made to mitigate the immense computational load of large-scale neural simulations by judicious simplification (Wang and Buzsáki, 1996; Bartos et al., 2002; Santhakumar et al., 2005; Eppler, 2008, Cutsuridis et al., 2010; Nowotny et al., 2014; Bezaire et al., 2016; Yavuz et al., 2016; Teeter et al., 2018; Amsalem et al., 2020; Knight et al., 2021; Knight and Nowotny, 2021, Wybo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by numerous citations to studies employing simplification strategies.

claim: Simplification inevitably results in feature or information loss, such as sacrificing multicompartmental information for simulation speed.
source: However, simplification inevitably results in feature or information loss, such as sacrificing multicompartmental information for simulation speed (Wang and Buzsáki, 1996; Bartos et al., 2002; Santhakumar et al., 2005; Bezaire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a known trade-off in computational modeling, supported by citations.

claim: Many fields have recently adopted various machine learning algorithms to counteract the increasing computational burden of ever-growing datasets on more traditional models.
source: To counteract the increasing computational burden of ever-growing datasets on more traditional models, many fields have recently adopted various machine learning algorithms (Sharma et al., 2011; Montavon et al., 2013; Meredig et al., 2014; Merembayev et al., 2018; Schütt et al., 2020).
evidence: This trend is supported by citations to machine learning applications across fields.

claim: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are superior to conventional model systems both in terms of speed and accuracy when dealing with complex systems such as those governing global financial markets or weather patterns.
source: Specifically, artificial neural networks (ANNs) are superior to conventional model systems both in terms of speed and accuracy when dealing with complex systems such as those governing global financial markets or weather patterns (Holmstrom, 2016; Ghoddusi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating ANN performance.

claim: The idea that individual neural cells could be represented by ANNs was proposed almost two decades ago.
source: The idea that individual neural cells could be represented by ANNs was proposed almost two decades ago (Poirazi et al., 2003); however, current ANN solutions are still unfit to replace traditional modeling systems as they cannot generate gradational neuronal dynamics needed for network simulations.
evidence: This historical claim is supported by a citation to Poirazi et al., 2003.

claim: Current ANN solutions are still unfit to replace traditional modeling systems as they cannot generate gradational neuronal dynamics needed for network simulations.
source: The idea that individual neural cells could be represented by ANNs was proposed almost two decades ago (Poirazi et al., 2003); however, current ANN solutions are still unfit to replace traditional modeling systems as they cannot generate gradational neuronal dynamics needed for network simulations.
evidence: This is presented as a limitation of existing ANN approaches at the time of writing.

claim: The linear and nonlinear models predicted subsequent membrane potential values with low error rates.
source: We found that both the linear and nonlinear models predicted subsequent membrane potential values with low error rates (Figure 1B) with similar behavior in both the CNN-LSTM and convolutional architectures (2.16 * 10–4 ± 1.18 * 10–3, 2.07 * 10–4 ± 1.11 * 10–3, 1.43 * 10–4 ± 9.31 * 10–4, 1.29 * 10–4 ± 9.42 * 10–4 mean error for linear, nonlinear, CNN-LSTM, and convolutional models, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental results with specific error measurements.

claim: The deep neural network performed considerably worse than all other tested models.
source: However, the deep neural network performed considerably worse than all other tested models (3.94 * 10–4 ± 1.56 * 10–3 mean error), potentially due to the nonlinear correspondence of its predicted values to the ground truth data (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental results with specific error measurements.

claim: Continuous predictions of the linear, convolutional, and CNN-LSTM models could explain the ground truth signal variance at high accuracy.
source: As expected from the fit error rates of single-membrane potential forecasting (Figure 1D), continuous predictions of the linear, convolutional, and CNN-LSTM models could explain the ground truth signal variance at high accuracy.
evidence: This is a finding from continuous prediction experiments.

claim: The nonlinear model produced the worst prediction for passive membrane potential traces despite performing the best on the benchmark dataset.
source: Surprisingly, the nonlinear model produced the worst prediction for passive membrane potential traces (0.82 ± 0.03 variance explained, n = 50) despite performing the best on the benchmark dataset.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental results.

claim: Only the CNN-LSTM architecture could precisely reproduce both subthreshold membrane potential dynamics and spiking activity.
source: Interestingly, we found that only the CNN-LSTM architecture could precisely reproduce both subthreshold membrane potential dynamics and spiking activity, while all other tested ANNs converged to the mean of the training dataset (Figure 1F and G, 4.4 ± 7.2%, 4.1 ± 6.9%, 0.5 ± 3.9%, 78.9 ± 6.7%, 4.4 ± 2.8% variance explained for linear, nonlinear, convolutional net and CNN-LSTM, deep neural net architectures, respectively, n = 50).
evidence: This is a key finding from the experimental results with quantitative measurements.

claim: The CNN-LSTM models correctly learned thresholding as the occurrence of the APs matched the timing of the testing dataset.
source: Closer inspection of the timing of the predicted APs revealed that the CNN-LSTM models correctly learned thresholding as the occurrence of the APs matched the timing of the testing dataset (Figure 1H; 83.94 ± 16.89% precision and 90.94 ± 12.13% recall, 0.24 ± 0.79 ms temporal shift for true-positive spikes compared to ground truth, n = 283), thus CNN-LSTM predictions yielded voltage traces with good initial agreement to NEURON signals.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from spike timing analysis.

claim: During extended 25 s simulation, there was no significant deviation from the ground truth signal in terms of explained variance or absolute difference.
source: During this extended simulation, we did not observe significant deviation from the ground truth signal in terms of explained variance (Figure 1J) or absolute difference (Figure 1K) and these metrics even improved slightly.
evidence: This is a finding from long-term stability testing.

claim: The CNN-LSTM responded linearly in subthreshold voltage regimes and elicited an AP after reaching threshold when administered excitatory inputs with variable quantal sizes.
source: Similar to the control NEURON model, the CNN-LSTM responded linearly in subthreshold voltage regimes (Figure 2A, Pearson's r = 0.99, n = 35) and elicited an AP after reaching threshold.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from generalization testing.

claim: The independently simulated NEURON model displayed similar temporal summation patterns to the CNN-LSTM for both sub- and suprathreshold events.
source: We found that the independently simulated NEURON model displayed similar temporal summation patterns to the CNN-LSTM for both sub- and suprathreshold events (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal summation testing.

claim: The predictions of the CNN-LSTM architecture closely matched traces obtained from the NEURON model when delivered unique temporal patterns of synaptic inputs with variable synaptic conductances.
source: Again, the predictions of the CNN-LSTM architecture closely matched traces obtained from the NEURON model (Figure 2D, Pearson's r = 0.81, n = 5000 ms) and the timing of the majority of the APs agreed with the ground truth data (91.02 ± 16.03% recall and 69.38 ± 22.43% precision, n = 50).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from generalization testing with variable inputs.

claim: The firing rate of the model did not scale linearly with the number of synapses in the presence of inhibitory inputs.
source: We noticed that the firing rate of this model did not scale linearly with the number of synapses as initially expected in the presence of inhibitory inputs (Enoki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, with a citation to expected behavior.

claim: The logistic function representing divisive normalization best fit the firing rate results.
source: We found that the logistic function representing divisive normalization best fit our results (Bhatia et al., 2019) (Akaike information criterion [AIC] for linear models representing subtractive and divisive inhibition versus AIC for logistic function: 983.3 ± 231.66 and 905.87 ± 200.92, respectively, n = 700 each).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from model fitting with AIC comparison.

claim: The CNN-LSTM model was able to replicate firing responses to variable synaptic conditions.
source: Notably, the CNN-LSTM model was able to replicate firing responses to these variable synaptic conditions (R2 values when comparing logistic fits for NEURON and CNN-LSTM models in 2:1 excitation–inhibition ratio: 0.996, for 1:2 excitation–inhibition ratio: 0.9, n = 700), further demonstrating the ability of the neuronal net to reproduce key features of neuronal excitability without prior entrainment.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from testing with variable excitation-inhibition ratios.

claim: Nonlinear signal summation at different subthreshold voltages was noted after shifting the steady-state activation and inactivation of the K+ conductance.
source: Nonlinear signal summation at different subthreshold voltages was noted after shifting the steady-state activation and inactivation of the K+ conductance (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with altered K+ conductance.

claim: All three models (control and shifted K+ conditions) were in good agreement with the NEURON simulation results and provided similar deviations in subthreshold membrane potential regimes compared to control conditions.
source: All three models were in good agreement with the NEURON simulation results and provided similar deviations in subthreshold membrane potential regimes compared to control conditions (Figure 2G and H, below resting membrane potential: –0.13 ± 0.36, –0.11 ± 0.03, –0.01 ± 0.23, 0.01 ± 0.06; above resting membrane potential: –0.4 ± 0.43, –0.22 ± 0.55, 0.35 ± 0.27, 0.2 ± 0.1 for CNN-LSTM right-shift, NEURON right-shift, CNN-LSTM left-shift, and NEURON left-shift, respectively, n = 270), indicating that CNN-LSTM can be rapidly adapted to account for biophysical alterations.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from testing with biophysical alterations.

claim: The accuracy of the CNN-LSTM prediction for ionic currents was similar to membrane potential predictions.
source: The accuracy of the CNN-LSTM prediction for these ionic currents was similar to membrane potential predictions (Figure 3, Pearson's r = 0.999 and 0.99 for fitting, n = 5000, variance explained: 15.1 ± 11.6% and 82 ± 6.1%; prediction correlation coefficient: 0.85 ± 0.08 and 0.81 ± 0.1, n = 5, for IK and INa, respectively) while the other ANNs again regressed to the mean.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ionic current prediction experiments.

claim: The CNN-LSTM architecture recreated the nonlinear response amplitude and time-course characteristic of AMPA-NMDA synapse activation.
source: Importantly, the CNN-LSTM architecture recreated the nonlinear response amplitude and time-course characteristic of AMPA-NMDA synapse activation (Schiller et al., 2000; Major et al., 2008; Branco and Häusser, 2011; Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from testing with NMDA receptors, with citations to expected behavior.

claim: Both NEURON and ANN models exhibited strongly boosted excitatory signals within a well-defined ISI time window (±12 ms) when NMDA-AMPA receptors were activated, which could produce APs.
source: We found that both NEURON and ANN models exhibited strongly boosted excitatory signals within a well-defined ISI time window (±12 ms) when NMDA-AMPA receptors were activated, which could produce APs.
evidence: This is a finding from coincidence detection testing.

claim: Across several NMDA conditions, output in the NEURON and ANN models was indistinguishable.
source: Across several NMDA conditions, output in the NEURON and ANN models was indistinguishable (Figure 4C, 12.42 ± 1.36 and 12.39 ± 2.3 Hz firing, respectively, in condition where 100% synapses contained NMDA receptors, n = 50).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from testing with varying NMDA content.

claim: The trained CNN-LSTM performed in near-perfect accordance with the NEURON simulation for the L5 pyramidal cell model.
source: We found that the trained CNN-LSTM performed in near-perfect accordance with the NEURON simulation (Figure 5A, Pearson's r = 0.999, n = 45,000 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from fitting the multicompartmental model.

claim: The continuous self-reliant prediction yielded lower yet adequate AP fidelity compared to the point neuron.
source: The continuous self-reliant prediction yielded lower yet adequate AP fidelity (Figure 5G, 68.28 ± 18.97% and 66.52 ± 25.37% precision and recall, 0.439 ± 4.181 ms temporal shift for true-positive spikes compared to ground truth, n = 205) compared to the point neuron, and the accuracy of subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations remained high (Pearson's r = 0.83, n = 37).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from continuous prediction testing of the L5 PC model.

claim: Only a small fraction of optimized filter weights were selected for robust information representation (13.83% of all weights were larger than 0.85), while the majority of them were closer to zero.
source: Despite the random initialization of these filters from a uniform distribution (He et al., 2015), only a small fraction of optimized filter weights were selected for robust information representation (13.83% of all weights were larger than 0.85), while the majority of them were closer to zero (Figure 5C), suggesting relevant feature selection.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the convolutional layer weights.

claim: Each synaptic input was assigned an independent selectivity filter.
source: We found that each synaptic input was assigned an independent selectivity filter (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of filter specificity.

claim: The comparison of mean weights of each synapse with the somatic amplitude revealed a flat linear correspondence (Pearson's r = 0.06), confirming that distal and proximal synaptic inputs carry equally relevant information for the CNN-LSTM.
source: This comparison revealed a flat linear correspondence (Pearson's r = 0.06), which combined with the filter specificity (Figure 5D) confirmed that distal and proximal synaptic inputs carry equally relevant information for the CNN-LSTM.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of synaptic weight distribution.

claim: The CNN-LSTM could determine at the first layer that excitatory and inhibitory inputs have opposing effects on subsequent membrane potential.
source: When comparing the weights of excitatory and inhibitory inputs, we found that even at the first layer the CNN-LSTM could determine that these inputs have opposing effects on subsequent membrane potential (5.91 * 10–6, 2.66 * 10–5, –6.22 * 10–6, and –1.34 * 10–5 mean weights for apical excitatory, basal excitatory, apical inhibitory, and basal inhibitory synapses, respectively, n = 51,200, 25,600, 15,360, and 10,240) even though these vectors only contain synaptic conductance information (comparable positive values for both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of excitatory vs inhibitory weights.

claim: ANNs were fit adequately to the NEURON simulations for layer 2/3, layer 4, and layer 6 PCs.
source: We found that the resulting ANNs were fit adequately to the NEURON simulations (Figure 5I, 94.2 ± 14.2%, 74.5 ± 23.5%, and 67 ± 14.5% variance explained, 86.6 ± 23.1%, 70.1 ± 25.8%, and 63.2 ± 33.2% precision, 90.7 ± 18%, 74.5 ± 25.8%, and 63.5 ± 32.7% recall for layer 2/3, layer 4, and layer 6 PCs, respectively, n = 50), and the fitting procedure was devoid of ambiguities.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from fitting ANNs to different cortical PC types.

claim: The custom ANN layer could reproduce a wide range of naturally occurring firing patterns.
source: The custom ANN layer (Figure 6A) could reproduce a wide range of naturally occurring firing patterns (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from testing the custom Izhikevich layer.

claim: The custom ANN layer could reliably capture the input–output characteristics of the NEURON model (Pearson's r: 0.982).
source: We found that the custom ANN layer could reliably capture the input–output characteristics of the NEURON model (Pearson's r: 0.982).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from testing the custom layer on a fast-spiking model.

claim: The custom ANN layer produced voltage responses in good agreement with the NEURON model (Pearson's r: 0.999, 96.9 ± 0.4% variance explained, n = 17).
source: The custom ANN layer produced voltage responses in good agreement with the NEURON model (Figure 6E and F, Pearson's r: 0.999, 96.9 ± 0.4% variance explained, n = 17).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from testing the custom layer with synaptic inputs.

claim: For point neurons, single-cell simulations ran significantly faster in NEURON than their CNN-LSTM counterparts when the optional initialization step was omitted.
source: For point neurons, single-cell simulations ran significantly faster in NEURON than their CNN-LSTM counterparts when the optional initialization step was omitted (Figure 7B, 3.68 ± 0.24 s, 0.65 ± 0.03 s, 2.19 ± 0.69 ms, and 0.72 ± 0.04 s, 100 ms cellular activity by NEURON with initialization, NEURON without initialization, CNN-LSTM on CPU, and CNN-LSTM on GPU, respectively, n = 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from runtime comparison experiments.

claim: When increasing the number of cells to 50, the predicted optimal scaling of CNN-LSTM models resulted in faster runtimes compared to NEURON models.
source: However, when increasing the number of cells, the predicted optimal scaling of CNN-LSTM models resulted in faster runtimes compared to NEURON models (e.g., for 50 cells, 24.23 ± 1.12 s, 7.45 ± 0.37 s, 4.42 ± 0.77 s, and 0.71 ± 0.05 s for a 100 ms simulation by NEURON with initialization, NEURON without initialization, CNN-LSTM on CPU, and CNN-LSTM on GPU, respectively, n = 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from runtime comparison with multiple cells.

claim: For 5000 point neurons, the NEURON simulation was ~148 times slower than a single-cell simulation, while the large-scale CNN-LSTM simulation was only four times slower than that of a single cell.
source: In these conditions, the NEURON simulation was ~148 times slower than a single-cell simulation. Notably, this large-scale CNN-LSTM simulation was only four times slower than that of a single cell (Figure 7B, 546.85 ± 4.61 ms, 407.2 ± 9 ms, 222.15458 ± 19.02 ms, and 2.97 ± 0.02ms for simulating 100 ms activity by NEURON with initialization, NEURON without initialization, CNN-LSTM on CPU, and CNN-LSTM on GPU, respectively, n = 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from large-scale runtime comparison.

claim: The single-cell simulation of the L5 PC model ran significantly slower than the CNN-LSTM abstraction.
source: We found that the single-cell simulation of the L5 PC model ran significantly slower than the CNN-LSTM abstraction (2.08 * 103 ± 84.66 s, 185.5 ± 3.7 s, 4.73 ± 0.13 s, and 1.02 ± 0.05 s for simulating 100 ms activity by NEURON with initialization, NEURON without initialization, CNN-LSTM on CPU, and CNN-LSTM on GPU, respectively, n = 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from runtime comparison of detailed biophysical models.

claim: For mid-sized simulations (50 L5 PCs), the runtime disparity resulted in a four to five orders of magnitude faster runtime for the CNN-LSTM.
source: This runtime disparity was markedly amplified in simulations with multiple cells (50 cells: 6.3 * 104 s, 5.8 * 103 s, 14.3 ± 0.24 s, and 1.19 ± 0.08 s, 5000 cells: 6.53 * 106 s, 6.28 * 105 s, 901.15 s, and 11.99 s for simulating 100 ms activity by NEURON with initialization, NEURON without initialization, CNN-LSTM on CPU, and CNN-LSTM on GPU respectively, n = 5), resulting in a four to five orders of magnitude faster runtime (depending on initialization) for the CNN-LSTM in case of mid-sized simulations.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from runtime comparison with multiple detailed cells.

claim: Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked methyl-CpG binding protein (MeCP2).
source: Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked methyl-CpG binding protein (MeCP2) (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rett syndrome, supported by a citation.

claim: Rett syndrome occurs in ~1:10,000 births worldwide, resulting in intellectual disability, dysmorphisms, declining cortical and motor function, stereotypies, and frequent myoclonic seizures, mostly in girls.
source: Rett syndrome occurs in ~1:10,000 births worldwide, resulting in intellectual disability, dysmorphisms, declining cortical and motor function, stereotypies, and frequent myoclonic seizures, mostly in girls (Belichenko et al., 1994; Armstrong, 1997; Steffenburg et al., 2001; Armstrong, 2002; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Fukuda et al., 2005; Belichenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rett syndrome prevalence and symptoms, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Changes in synaptic transmission, morphological alterations in neurons, and altered network connectivity have been reported in Rett syndrome.
source: Although the underlying cellular and network mechanisms are largely unknown, changes in synaptic transmission (Dani et al., 2005; Medrihan et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010), morphological alterations in neurons (Akbarian et al., 2001; Kishi and Macklis, 2004), and altered network connectivity (Dani and Nelson, 2009) have been reported in Rett syndrome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rett syndrome pathology, supported by multiple citations.

claim: For a single simulation of the L5 microcircuit, CNN-LSTM models were more than 9300 times faster compared to NEURON models.
source: We found that for a single simulation, CNN-LSTM models were more than 9300 times faster compared to NEURON models (Figure 8C, 21.153 ± 0.26 s vs. 54.69 hr for CNN-LSTM and NEURON models, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from runtime comparison of the Rett syndrome network model.

claim: Both excitatory drive and recurrent connectivity had considerable influence over network instability in the Rett syndrome model.
source: By systematically changing excitatory quantal size (Dani et al., 2005) and the ratio of recurrent L5 PC innervation to mimic reduced recurrent connectivity and synaptic drive in Rett syndrome, we found that both alterations had considerable influence over network instability (Figure 9B, left panel; excitatory drive: 17.85 ± 61.61 vs. 388.92 ± 170.03 pre-stimulus APs for excitatory drive scaled by 0.75 and 1.25, respectively, n = 100 each, p<0.001; recurrent connectivity: 321.96 ± 200.42 vs. 157.66 ± 192.5 pre-stimulus APs for 10 and 5.2% recurrent connectivity, similar to reported values for adult wild-type and Mecp2-null mutant mice [Dani and Nelson, 2009], n = 50 each, p<0.001) and response to stimuli (excitatory drive: 147.58 ± 17.2 vs. 119.23 ± 18.1 APs upon stimulus for excitatory drive scaled by 0.75 and 1.25, respectively, n = 100 each, p=2.3 * 10–22, t(198) = 11.03, two-sample t-test; recurrent connectivity: 134.76 ± 21.37 vs. 112.74 ± 34.99 APs upon stimulus for 10 and 5.2% recurrent connectivity, n = 50 each, p=2.54 * 10–4, t(98) = 3.8, two-sample t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from parameter space mapping of the Rett syndrome model.

claim: When inhibitory quantal size was altered, inhibition had a negligible effect on network instability, as connectivity below 9% never resulted in oscillatory activity.
source: Contrary to disruption of the excitatory drive, when inhibitory quantal size (Chao et al., 2010) was altered, we found that inhibition had a negligible effect on network instability, as connectivity below 9% never resulted in oscillatory activity (Figure 9—figure supplement 1; inhibition corresponds to random inhibitory drive, as the network did not contain ANNs representing feed-forward inhibitory cells).
evidence: This is a finding from parameter space mapping with altered inhibition.

claim: Recurrent connectivity observed in young Mecp2-null mice (7.8%) yielded more stable microcircuits (54% of networks were stable, n = 100) than wild-type conditions (34% of networks were stable, n = 50).
source: Specifically, recurrent connectivity observed in young Mecp2-null mice (7.8%; Dani and Nelson, 2009) yielded more stable microcircuits (54% of networks were stable, n = 100) than wild-type conditions (34% of networks were stable, n = 50).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the Rett syndrome network model.

claim: Recurrent connection probability of older animals (5.3%) further stabilized the network (64% of networks were stable).
source: Recurrent connection probability of older animals (5.3%) further stabilized this network (64% of networks were stable).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the Rett syndrome network model.

claim: The model suggests that reduced recurrent connectivity between L5 PCs is not causal to seizure generation and abnormal network activity in Rett syndrome.
source: Taken together, our model suggests that reduced recurrent connectivity between L5 PCs is not causal to seizure generation and abnormal network activity (Steffenburg et al., 2001; Roche et al., 2019), which are crucial symptoms of Rett syndrome at a young age, but instead normal PC activation is disrupted.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results, with citations to clinical observations.

claim: The CNN-LSTM is the only model that could depict the full dynamic range of a biophysical neural model among the tested ANN architectures.
source: Consequently, of the tested ANN architectures, the CNN-LSTM is the only model that could depict the full dynamic range of a biophysical neural model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative testing of different ANN architectures.

claim: ANNs do not require hard-coding of the governing rules for neuronal signal processing.
source: First, ANNs do not require hard-coding of the governing rules for neuronal signal processing.
evidence: This is a known property of ANNs.

claim: ANNs can derive the main principles of input–output processing and neglect otherwise unimpactful processes.
source: Upon creation, ANNs serve as a blank canvas that can derive the main principles of input–output processing and neglect otherwise unimpactful processes (Benitez et al., 1997; Dayhoff and DeLeo, 2001; Castelvecchi, 2016).
evidence: This is a known property of ANNs, supported by citations.

claim: The CNN-LSTM architecture represents the first ANN implementation that can serve as a viable alternate for biophysically and morphologically realistic neurons in a network model environment.
source: Our ANN architecture fulfills these requirements, thus representing the first ANN implementation that can serve as a viable alternate for biophysically and morphologically realistic neurons in a network model environment.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: ANN training can last up to 24 hr to achieve accurate fits.
source: First, although ANN training can be carried out on affordable and widely available resources, training times can last up to 24 hr to achieve accurate fits ('Methods').
evidence: This is a practical observation about the training process.

claim: The 1 ms temporal discretization hinders the implementation of certain biological phenomena that operate on much faster timescales, such as gap junctions.
source: Additionally, the 1 ms temporal discretization hinders the implementation of certain biological phenomena that operate on much faster timescales, such as gap junctions.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the approach.

claim: The drastic runtime acceleration is the direct consequence of the parallelized graph-based ANN approach.
source: These results confirm that the drastic runtime acceleration is the direct consequence of the parallelized graph-based ANN approach.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the runtime comparison experiments.

claim: Excitatory transmission is bidirectionally modulated by MeCP2 knockout and overexpression.
source: Excitatory transmission is bidirectionally modulated by MeCP2 knockout (Nelson et al., 2006; Chao et al., 2007) and overexpression (Na et al., 2012), and long-term synaptic plasticity is also impaired in MeCP2-deficient mice (Asaka et al., 2006; Guy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MeCP2 effects, supported by citations.

claim: MeCP2 directly regulates the number of glutamatergic synapses, amounting to a 39% reduction of putative excitatory synapses in the hippocampus and a 50% reduction in recurrent excitatory connections between L5 PCs.
source: This regulation amounts to a 39% reduction of putative excitatory synapses in the hippocampus (Chao et al., 2007) and a 50% reduction in recurrent excitatory connections between L5 PCs (Dani and Nelson, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MeCP2 effects on connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: Both constitutive and excitatory-cell-targeted MeCP2 mutations lead to network seizure generation as opposed to inhibitory-cell-targeted MeCP2 mutation, which causes frequent hyperexcitability discharges but never seizures.
source: These results are supported by previous findings showing that both constitutive (Calfa et al., 2011) and excitatory-cell-targeted (Zhang et al., 2014) MeCP2 mutations lead to network seizure generation as opposed to inhibitory-cell-targeted MeCP2 mutation, which causes frequent hyperexcitability discharges but never seizures (Chao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell-type-specific MeCP2 effects, supported by citations.

claim: Excitatory synaptic alterations in Rett affect both general network responses and network stability, which may serve as substrates to cognitive dysfunction and seizures, respectively.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that excitatory synaptic alterations in Rett affect both general network responses and network stability, which may serve as substrates to cognitive dysfunction and seizures, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.
